claims.claim: An elaborate ancestral cerebral organization was already present in the lower Cambrian.
claims.source: The earlier identification of a hexapod-malacostracan-like brain in a fossil stem arthropod (Ma et al., 2015) together with the present results argues for an elaborate ancestral cerebral organization already present in the lower Cambrian.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on fossil evidence and the current findings.

claims.claim: In stomatopods, the brain's lateral protocerebra are contained within the distal eyestalks.
claims.source: In stomatopods, as in most stalk-eyed crustaceans, the brain's lateral protocerebra are contained within the distal eyestalks (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The lateral protocerebra in mantis shrimps are exceptionally capacious due to the voluminous nested optic lobe neuropils.
claims.source: These are exceptionally capacious in mantis shrimps due to the voluminous nested optic lobe neuropils, which serve the largest and most complex compound eyes yet described (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Mantis shrimps have the largest and most complex compound eyes yet described.
claims.source: These are exceptionally capacious in mantis shrimps due to the voluminous nested optic lobe neuropils, which serve the largest and most complex compound eyes yet described (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the image in Figure 1A and is consistent with known literature on stomatopod vision.

claims.claim: In the mantis shrimp, the largest neuropil of the lateral protocerebrum originates from a dorsal cell body cluster of about 170,000 minute and tightly clustered neuronal perikarya.
claims.source: In the mantis shrimp, the largest of these neuropils originates from a dorsal cell body cluster of about 170,000 (in N. oerstedii) minute and tightly clustered neuronal perikarya, which we here refer to as globuli cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on cell counts from the study.

claims.claim: The globuli cell population in mantis shrimps provides the neurons that form four columnar neuropils, each comprising thousands of parallel fibers.
claims.source: This population provides the neurons that form four columnar neuropils, each comprising thousands of parallel fibers.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claims.claim: Only one of the four columns in mantis shrimps is surmounted by a large calyx-like neuropil.
claims.source: Only one of the four columns is surmounted by a large calyx-like neuropil (Figure 1D) composed of layers of dendritic arborizations.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The large calyx-like neuropil in mantis shrimps is composed of layers of dendritic arborizations.
claims.source: Only one of the four columns is surmounted by a large calyx-like neuropil (Figure 1D) composed of layers of dendritic arborizations.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The four columns in mantis shrimps extend latero-caudally and together demarcate the proximal margin of the eyestalk neuropil, near its junction with the eyestalk nerve.
claims.source: The four columns (Figure 1E), which extend latero-caudally, together demarcate the proximal margin of the eyestalk neuropil, near its junction with the eyestalk nerve (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figures 1C and 1E.

claims.claim: Globuli cells in mantis shrimps provide one very large dome-like neuropil (calyx) from which one of the smaller columns originates.
claims.source: Globuli cells provide one very large dome-like neuropil (here termed the calyx, indicated Ca in Figure 1D,E) from which one of the smaller columns originates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by figures.

claims.claim: Globuli cells in mantis shrimps also provide parallel fibers constituting three additional columns.
claims.source: Globuli cells also provide parallel fibers constituting three additional columns (Figure 1E; Figure 2B,C), one of which is equipped with a small calyx distally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by figures.

claims.claim: One of the three additional columns in mantis shrimps is equipped with a small calyx distally.
claims.source: Globuli cells also provide parallel fibers constituting three additional columns (Figure 1E; Figure 2B,C), one of which is equipped with a small calyx distally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Two of the columns in mantis shrimps lack distal dendrites entirely.
claims.source: The two other columns lack distal dendrites entirely.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claims.claim: Neurites from globuli cells converge at the origin of each column in mantis shrimps, as they do at the pedunculus of an insect mushroom body.
claims.source: Neurites from globuli cells converge at the origin of each column, as they do at the pedunculus (or initial stalk) of an insect mushroom body (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by figures.

claims.claim: Each globuli cell neurite in mantis shrimps increases in girth and extends for hundreds of microns as a thicker process decorated with varicosities and spines representing pre- and postsynaptic sites.
claims.source: Each cell body neurite then increases in girth and extends for hundreds of microns as a thicker process decorated with varicosities and spines representing, respectively, pre- and postsynaptic sites (Strausfeld and Meinertzhagen, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation, with citation supporting the interpretation of varicosities and spines.

claims.claim: Globuli cells in stomatopods lack a proper axon; each globuli cell's parallel fiber serves as a local interneuron.
claims.source: Like Kenyon cells in insect mushroom bodies, globuli cells in stomatopods lack a proper axon: each globuli cell's parallel fiber serves as a local interneuron, corresponding in shape and decoration to the parallel fibers of the insect mushroom body lobes, exemplified by D. melanogaster (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Each parallel fiber in stomatopods is assumed to contribute to local computational circuits within its column.
claims.source: And by comparison to the Drosophila mushroom body lobe, each parallel fiber is assumed to contribute to local computational circuits within its column (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with Drosophila, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Parallel fibers in both stomatopods and cockroaches are regularly intersected by the branched processes of efferent and afferent neurons.
claims.source: Comparing the columns of the stomatopod mushroom body and the mushroom body lobes of the cockroach Periplaneta americana (Figure 1G,H) further demonstrates that parallel fibers in both species are regularly intersected by the branched processes of efferent and afferent neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by Figures 1G and 1H.

claims.claim: In the stomatopod mushroom body, orthogonally organized neurons and local circuits provided by parallel fibers offer many thousands of possible sensory associations.
claims.source: As in the insect mushroom body, in the stomatopod mushroom body orthogonally organized neurons and local circuits provided by parallel fibers (Figure 1H) offer many thousands of possible sensory associations (Heisenberg, 2003; Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007; Huerta et al., 2004; Aso et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations and supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: In insects, the packing density of globuli cells associated with a mushroom body exceeds the packing density of neuronal cell bodies elsewhere in the brain.
claims.source: In insects, the packing density of globuli cells associated with a mushroom body exceeds the packing density of neuronal cell bodies elsewhere in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is a known characteristic of insect mushroom bodies.

claims.claim: The packing density of globuli cells supplying the stomatopod mushroom body is comparable to that of globuli cells supplying the mushroom bodies of insects.
claims.source: Our measurements show that the packing density of globuli cells supplying the stomatopod mushroom body is comparable to that of globuli cells supplying the mushroom bodies of insects, here exemplified by P. americana (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from the study, supported by Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Clawed specializations that partially wrap around large terminal boutons of sensory afferents are an important identifier of mushroom bodies in insects.
claims.source: An important identifier of mushroom bodies in insects is the morphology of its Kenyon cells and their specializations; in particular, clawed specializations that partially wrap around large terminal boutons of sensory afferents in the calyces of flies and other insects (Yasuyama et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on insect mushroom body morphology.

claims.claim: Clawed specializations are identified in stomatopods, but only on dendrites contributing to the smaller of the two calyces.
claims.source: These are also identified in stomatopods, but only on dendrites contributing to the smaller of the two calyces (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In the larger calyx of stomatopods, spined dendritic processes correspond to the spined dendrites of the mushroom body calyx of P. americana.
claims.source: In the larger calyx, spined dendritic processes correspond to the spined dendrites of the mushroom body calyx of P. americana (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The stomatopod calyx is deeper than an insect calyx and is composed of four distinct levels.
claims.source: However, the stomatopod calyx is deeper than is an insect calyx and is composed of four distinct levels, the second of which is characterized by hundreds of thousands of synaptic clusters comparable to microglomeruli identified in the calyces of insects (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The second level of the stomatopod calyx is characterized by hundreds of thousands of synaptic clusters comparable to microglomeruli identified in the calyces of insects.
claims.source: However, the stomatopod calyx is deeper than is an insect calyx and is composed of four distinct levels, the second of which is characterized by hundreds of thousands of synaptic clusters comparable to microglomeruli identified in the calyces of insects (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In insects, the processes of uniquely identifiable efferent and afferent neurons are arranged at specific loci along the length of a mushroom body's lobe, giving the lobe the appearance of being segmented into discrete synaptic domains.
claims.source: In insects, the processes of uniquely identifiable efferent and afferent neurons are arranged at specific loci along the length of a mushroom body's lobe, giving the lobe the appearance of being segmented into discrete synaptic domains (Li and Strausfeld, 1999; Ito et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on insect mushroom body organization.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, neurons at specific loci along the lobes have been shown to encode the adaptive values of sensory information associated with learned responses.
claims.source: In Drosophila, such neurons at specific loci along the lobes have been shown to encode the adaptive values of sensory information associated with learned responses (Aso et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study in Drosophila.

claims.claim: The same type of organization (segmented synaptic domains) typifies the stomatopod mushroom body columns.
claims.source: The same type of organization typifies the stomatopod mushroom body columns (Figure 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figures 2E and 2F.

claims.claim: In N. oerstedii, GAD-immunoreactive neurons extending across the two largest columns are representative of centrifugal pathways back to the calyx.
claims.source: In N. oerstedii GAD-immunoreactive neurons extending across the two largest columns are representative of centrifugal pathways back to the calyx (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Aminergic afferents in stomatopods demonstrate discrete territories along the length of the mushroom body columns.
claims.source: Other aminergic afferents are resolved using antisera against serotonin (5HT) and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH). These also demonstrate discrete territories along the length of the mushroom body columns (Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figures 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: TH-immunoreactive neurons in stomatopods correspond to discrete dopaminergic territories in the mushroom body of D. melanogaster.
claims.source: These arrangements of TH-immunoreactive neurons, first identified in the mushroom body lobes of the fly Calliphora erythrocephala (Nässel and Elekes, 1992), correspond to discrete dopaminergic territories in the mushroom body of D. melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: Thermogenetics, optogenetics, and mutant analysis have demonstrated the pivotal role of dopaminergic neurons in appetitive and aversive conditioning in Drosophila.
claims.source: Thermogenetics, optogenetics, and mutant analysis have demonstrated the pivotal role of these neurons in appetitive and aversive conditioning (Waddell, 2013; Waddell, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies in Drosophila.

claims.claim: Three-dimensional reconstructions of the stomatopod mushroom bodies confirm that only one of the four columns originates from the extensive volume of dendritic processes that constitute the elaborate calyx.
claims.source: Three-dimensional reconstructions of the stomatopod mushroom bodies confirm that only one of the four columns (Clm 3, Figure 2B) originates from the extensive volume of dendritic processes that constitute the elaborate calyx (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from the study, supported by Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Golgi impregnations resolve a smaller column capped by a much smaller cluster of outer dendrites constituting a second calyx in stomatopods.
claims.source: Golgi impregnations resolve a smaller column (Clm 4) capped by a much smaller cluster of outer dendrites constituting a second calyx.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from Golgi impregnations.

claims.claim: The remaining two columns in stomatopods are the largest and are composed of 'naked' globuli cells entirely lacking distal dendrites.
claims.source: The remaining two columns (Clm 1, 2) are the largest and are composed of 'naked' globuli cells entirely lacking distal dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: All four columns in stomatopods are supplied by globuli cells.
claims.source: That all four columns are supplied by globuli cells is another correspondence with the organization of the insect mushroom body, which develops from four cell lineages, the clonal progeny of which do not remain separated but merge to form a single neuropil (Ito et al., 1997; Farris et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation, with citation supporting the comparison to insects.

claims.claim: The insect mushroom body develops from four cell lineages, the clonal progeny of which do not remain separated but merge to form a single neuropil.
claims.source: That all four columns are supplied by globuli cells is another correspondence with the organization of the insect mushroom body, which develops from four cell lineages, the clonal progeny of which do not remain separated but merge to form a single neuropil (Ito et al., 1997; Farris et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies in insects.

claims.claim: In the mantis shrimp, four distinct columns originate from the same globuli cell population but remain separate from each other.
claims.source: In the mantis shrimp, four distinct columns originate from the same globuli cell population but remain separate from each other (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by figures.

claims.claim: The absence of a cap or calyx crowning two of the stomatopod mushroom body columns is comparable to the organization of mushroom bodies in palaeopteran insects (mayflies, damselflies), which entirely lack calyces.
claims.source: The absence of a cap or calyx crowning two of the stomatopod mushroom body columns is comparable to the organization of mushroom bodies in palaeopteran insects (mayflies, damselflies), which entirely lack calyces (Strausfeld et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: The 'calyxless' condition typifies mushroom bodies in Myriapoda.
claims.source: This 'calyxless' condition also typifies mushroom bodies in Myriapoda, another mandibulate taxon (Wolff and Strausfeld, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claims.claim: Ancestral morphology is suggested by mushroom body development in insects, where outgrowth of the lobes precedes the development of the calyx.
claims.source: Ancestral morphology is also suggested by mushroom body development in insects, where outgrowth of the lobes precedes the development of the calyx (Ito et al., 1997; Farris et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on developmental studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The stomatopod mushroom body columns and the insect mushroom body lobes are recognized at the molecular level by antibodies raised against three proteins required for learning and memory in Drosophila: DC0, Leonardo, and pCaMKII.
claims.source: To summarize, the combination of neuroanatomical characters that distinguish the insect mushroom body also distinguish the stomatopod mushroom body (Table 1). Furthermore, the stomatopod mushroom body columns and the insect mushroom body lobes are recognized at the molecular level by antibodies raised against three proteins required for learning and memory in Drosophila: (1) protein kinase A catalytic subunit alpha (DC0) (Skoulakis et al., 1993), (2) Leonardo (Leo), the ortholog of mammalian 14-3-3ζ (Skoulakis and Davis, 1996), and (3) phosphorylated calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (pCaMKII) (Wang et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological data from the study, with citations supporting the functional significance of these proteins.

claims.claim: In the cockroach lateral protocerebrum, all three antibodies (DC0, Leo, pCaMKII) selectively resolve the mushroom body lobes.
claims.source: In the cockroach lateral protocerebrum, all three antibodies selectively resolve the mushroom body lobes (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 4F.

claims.claim: In the lateral protocerebrum of the stomatopod brain, the three antibodies (DC0, Leo, pCaMKII) selectively resolve all four columns.
claims.source: Similarly, in the lateral protocerebrum of the stomatopod brain these three antibodies selectively resolve all four columns identified by reduced silver staining and Golgi impregnation (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figures 4B-E.

claims.claim: Mapping brain morphologies onto a representative genomic phylogeny of Pancrustacea demonstrates the absence of mushroom bodies in all taxa intervening between the clade Hexapoda+Remipedia and Eumalacostraca.
claims.source: Mapping brain morphologies onto a representative genomic phylogeny of Pancrustacea (Oakley et al., 2013) demonstrates the absence of mushroom bodies in all taxa intervening between the clade Hexapoda+Remipedia and Eumalacostraca (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on a comparative analysis across taxa, supported by Figure 5A and citation to a phylogenetic study.

claims.claim: Alpheid caridids ('pistol shrimps') are the only group known to have evolved eusociality among crustaceans.
claims.source: Alpheid caridids ('pistol shrimps') are the only group known to have evolved eusociality.
claims.evidence: This is a known fact about pistol shrimp behavior.

claims.claim: Anti-DC0 resolves a pedestal-like extension from the domed hemiellipsoid body in the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus.
claims.source: In the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus (Stenopodidea), anti-DC0 resolves a pedestal-like extension from its domed hemiellipsoid body (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is divided into three distinct territories.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The pedestal-like extension from the hemiellipsoid body in Stenopus hispidus is divided into three distinct territories.
claims.source: In the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus (Stenopodidea), anti-DC0 resolves a pedestal-like extension from its domed hemiellipsoid body (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is divided into three distinct territories.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Anti-DC0 reveals prominent mushroom body-like centers in Alpheus bellulus (Caridea).
claims.source: Anti-DC0 also reveals prominent mushroom body-like centers in Alpheus bellulus (Caridea).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations from the study.

claims.claim: Golgi impregnations of A. bellulus show mushroom body-like centers prominently in the lateral protocerebrum where they are of comparable size to those of social or parasitoid hymenopteran insects.
claims.source: Golgi impregnations of A. bellulus show these prominently in the lateral protocerebrum where they are of comparable size to those of social or parasitoid hymenopteran insects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is based on Golgi impregnations from the study, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: In the land hermit crab C. clypeatus (Anomura), the hemiellipsoid body consists of an enormous domed neuropil characterized by concentrically arranged DC0- and pCaMKII-immunoreactive layers.
claims.source: The land hermit crab C. clypeatus (Anomura) is distinct: its hemiellipsoid body consists of an enormous domed neuropil that is characterized by concentrically arranged DC0- and pCaMKII-immunoreactive layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Each layer in the hemiellipsoid body of C. clypeatus is a flat sheet comprising a planar arrangement of globuli cell processes that are orthogonally intersected by the arborizations of input and output neurons.
claims.source: Each is a flat sheet comprising a planar arrangement of globuli cell processes that are orthogonally intersected by the arborizations of input and output neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claims.claim: The network organization within each layer of the C. clypeatus hemiellipsoid body corresponds to the three-dimensional networks defined by sequential domains of input and output arborizations in the insect mushroom body.
claims.source: Although these arrangements are peculiar to land hermit crabs, they demonstrate that the network organization within each layer corresponds to the three-dimensional networks that are defined by the sequential domains of input and output arborizations that extend across parallel fibers in the insect mushroom body (Brown and Wolff, 2012; Wolff et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations.

claims.claim: In crayfish (Astacidea), the dorsal globuli cell cluster provides a prominent domed center in the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.source: In crayfish (Astacidea), the dorsal globuli cell cluster provides a prominent domed center in the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claims.claim: The hemiellipsoid body of crayfish does not show discernable levels of the proteins involved in Drosophila learning and memory.
claims.source: However this hemiellipsoid body does not show discernable levels of the proteins involved in Drosophila learning and memory (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The hemiellipsoid bodies of the examined varunid crabs (Brachyura) are inconspicuous and lack elevated levels of learning and memory proteins.
claims.source: The hemiellipsoid bodies of the examined varunid crabs (Brachyura) are inconspicuous and they too lack elevated levels of those proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: More recently evolved Eumalacostraca show a reduction or complete loss of mushroom body-like lobes (columns), accompanied by accentuation and diversification of domed neuropils that have been historically referred to as hemiellipsoid bodies.
claims.source: Together, with other neuroanatomical criteria (Table 1), these observations suggest that more recently evolved Eumalacostraca show a reduction or complete loss of mushroom body-like lobes (columns), accompanied by accentuation and diversification of domed neuropils that have been historically referred to as hemiellipsoid bodies (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative neuroanatomical data, supported by Table 1 and Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The reniform body in N. oerstedii arises from a dense cluster of about a thousand cell bodies.
claims.source: This is the reniform body, a prominent compound neuropil located near the inner margin of the optic lobes (RB in Figure 1C), which in N. oerstedii arises from a dense cluster of about a thousand cell bodies.
claims.evidence: This is based on cell counts from the study, supported by Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The reniform body in N. oerstedii provides a pedestal-like arrangement of smooth parallel neurites supplying four domains: an initial zone and a lateral, distal, and proximal zone.
claims.source: These provide a pedestal-like arrangement of smooth parallel neurites supplying four domains: an initial zone and a lateral, distal, and proximal zone.
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation from the study.

claims.claim: All four zones of the reniform body contain the dendritic processes of collaterals branching from the pedestal as well as numerous branched afferent processes that supply them.
claims.source: All four zones contain the dendritic processes of collaterals branching from the pedestal as well as numerous branched afferent processes that supply them (Figure 6A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct anatomical observation supported by Figures 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: Anti-DC0 immunocytology demonstrates expression of this antigen in all four zones of the reniform body, but at a much lower level than seen in mushroom body columns.
claims.source: Anti-DC0 immunocytology demonstrates expression of this antigen in all four zones, but at a much lower level than seen in mushroom body columns (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The same center (reniform body) has been identified at the same location and orientation in the shore crabs Hemigrapsus nudus and H. oregonensis.
claims.source: The same center has been identified at the same location and orientation, with respect to the optic lobes, in the shore crabs Hemigrapsus nudus and H. oregonensis, again revealing domains corresponding to those of the reniform body in N. oerstedii.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation from the study.

claims.claim: In H. nudus, discrete neuropils in the lateral protocerebrum either lack discernable DC0 or express it at very low levels, with an exception being a tract of axons leading from the optic lobes centrally.
claims.source: However, in H. nudus, these and other discrete neuropils in the lateral protocerebrum either lack discernable DC0 or, if DC0 is expressed, it is at very low levels. An exception is a tract of axons leading from the optic lobes centrally (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunocytological observations supported by Figure 6H.

claims.claim: The reniform body has been erroneously identified as a mushroom body homologue.
claims.source: Superficially, the reniform body is suggestive of a mushroom body-like center due to the arrangement of parallel processes that make up its pedestal. It is this feature that has lead to its erroneous identification as a mushroom body homologue (Maza et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of a previous study, with citation.

claims.claim: It is broadly accepted that insects originated from crustaceans.
claims.source: It is broadly accepted that insects originated from crustaceans.

results.result: Stomatopod crustaceans (mantis shrimps) possess insect-like mushroom bodies characterized by a dorsal cluster of approximately 170,000 globuli cells that form four columnar neuropils composed of parallel fibers. Only one column is surmounted by a large calyx, one has a small calyx, and two lack distal dendrites entirely. The globuli cell packing density in stomatopods is comparable to that in insects.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C54-C68, C73, C86-C89, and C91 collectively provide detailed anatomical descriptions of stomatopod mushroom bodies based on direct observations using multiple techniques (silver staining, Golgi impregnation, 3D reconstruction, cell counts). The data are internally consistent, supported by figures, and demonstrate the presence of mushroom body-like structures in stomatopods with quantitative measurements of cell numbers and packing densities.

results.result: The stomatopod mushroom body columns exhibit organizational features characteristic of insect mushroom bodies, including parallel fibers intersected by efferent and afferent neurons forming orthogonal networks, clawed dendritic specializations, synaptic microglomeruli in the calyx, and segmented synaptic domains with aminergic (GAD, serotonin, tyrosine hydroxylase) innervation patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C84 describe detailed anatomical and neurochemical features observed through comparative analysis, immunocytology, and Golgi impregnations. The observations are supported by multiple figures showing orthogonal networks, clawed specializations, microglomeruli, and aminergic innervation patterns that parallel those in insects. The comparative approach strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Stomatopod mushroom body columns and insect mushroom body lobes are recognized at the molecular level by antibodies against three proteins required for learning and memory in Drosophila: DC0, Leonardo, and pCaMKII. These antibodies selectively resolve all four columns in stomatopods and the lobes in cockroaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by immunocytological data presented in Figure 4 and described in the text. The selective labeling of mushroom body structures by these three antibodies in both stomatopods and insects provides molecular evidence for functional similarity. The use of well-characterized antibodies with known specificity in Drosophila strengthens this result.

results.result: Comparative analysis across Eumalacostraca reveals that mushroom bodies are absent in taxa between Hexapoda+Remipedia and Eumalacostraca, but some mushroom body characters are present in Alpheoidea, Stenopodidea, and land hermit crabs. More recently evolved Eumalacostraca (Anomura, Astacidea, Brachyura) show reduction or loss of mushroom body columns accompanied by elaboration of domed hemiellipsoid bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C100-C110, C135-C136 are based on comparative neuroanatomical analysis of five decapod species using immunocytology (DC0, pCaMKII) and Golgi impregnations. The data are presented in Figure 5 and supplementary figures, showing a gradient of mushroom body-like features across taxa. The interpretation of evolutionary modification is consistent with the phylogenetic framework and anatomical observations.

results.result: The hemiellipsoid body has derived from an ancestral mushroom body, as suggested by the presence of some but not all mushroom body characters in the closest eumalacostracan relatives of stomatopods. The abundance of divergent hemiellipsoid body morphologies and taxon-specific olfactory innervation support interpretation of the hemiellipsoid body as a highly divergent mushroom body calyx.
results.evaluation: Claims C134 and C137 present an evolutionary interpretation based on comparative data (C110, C135-C136) and historical literature. While the comparative observations are supported, the inference that hemiellipsoid bodies derived from ancestral mushroom bodies rather than representing convergent evolution or independent structures requires additional evidence (e.g., developmental, molecular phylogenetic data). The interpretation is plausible but not definitively demonstrated.

results.result: The reniform body in stomatopods and shore crabs is a distinct visual association center that has been erroneously identified as a mushroom body homologue. It arises from approximately 1,000 cell bodies, provides smooth parallel neurites to four domains, and shows low DC0 expression. The structure described in Neohelice granulata by Maza et al. (2016) corresponds to the reniform body, not a mushroom body.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C148 provide detailed anatomical characterization of the reniform body in stomatopods and crabs, supported by Golgi impregnations, immunocytology, and comparative analysis (Figure 6). The critical evaluation of Maza et al. (2016) is based on specific anatomical criteria: smooth parallel fibers lacking spines/varicosities, absence of orthogonal networks, and restricted DC0 expression. The comparative data support the conclusion that the reniform body is distinct from mushroom bodies.

results.result: Two interpretations are possible for the presence of mushroom bodies in stomatopods and insects: convergent evolution or retention of an ancestral attribute. Fossil evidence from the lower Cambrian stem arthropod Fuxianhuia protensa suggests an elaborate ancestral cerebral organization. However, the sister groups of hexapods (Remipedia) and malacostracans (Leptostraca) possess hemiellipsoid bodies, not mushroom bodies, arguing against simple homology. Transcriptomic evaluation is needed for definitive resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C159, C177-C178 present alternative evolutionary hypotheses and acknowledge the limitations of current evidence. The fossil evidence (C151-C152) supports ancient complexity but cannot resolve internal brain organization. The phylogenetic distribution (C159) argues against simple homology. The authors appropriately conclude that definitive resolution requires transcriptomic data (C158), which is not yet available. This represents an honest assessment of uncertainty.

results.result: If mushroom bodies evolved convergently in stomatopods and insects, the selective constraint may relate to memory of exact locations for foraging rather than superior vision per se. Eumalacostracan groups with mushroom body-like attributes (cleaner shrimps, pistol shrimps, land hermit crabs) all exhibit behaviors requiring memory of specific locations, supporting this hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C172 present a hypothesis about selective pressures for mushroom body evolution based on behavioral correlations. While the behavioral observations are supported by citations (C166-C171), the causal link between location memory and mushroom body evolution is speculative. The counterexamples (C162-C164) showing dissociation between visual complexity and mushroom body presence strengthen the argument against vision as the primary driver, but the positive evidence for location memory as the driver is correlational rather than experimental.

results.result: Stomatopod and insect mushroom bodies pass three crucial tests for phenotypic homology: similarity (detailed anatomical correspondence), conjunction (exclusion of competing structures like reniform bodies), and congruence (co-existence of other homologous brain centers such as fan-shaped central complex neuropils).
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C176 apply established criteria for phenotypic homology (Patterson, 1988) to the comparative data. The similarity criterion is supported by the extensive anatomical data (Results 1-2). The conjunction criterion is supported by the demonstration that reniform bodies coexist with mushroom bodies in stomatopods (Result 6). The congruence criterion is supported by citation to additional shared brain structures (C176). The logical application of these criteria to the data is sound.

results.result: Mushroom bodies are the iconic learning and memory centers of insects, first identified in Hymenoptera in 1850. They are anatomically defined by specific features including parallel fibers from globuli cells forming a peduncle that divides into lobes, a calyx receiving sensory inputs (absent in some groups), inhibitory feedback pathways, and enriched expression of learning/memory proteins. Functionally, they mediate olfactory processing, appetitive/aversive memory, and spatial memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C25 provide background on insect mushroom bodies based on well-established literature. These claims are supported by multiple citations to authoritative studies and represent consensus knowledge in the field. They establish the baseline criteria for identifying mushroom bodies in other taxa.

results.result: No previously described crustacean possesses a mushroom body as defined by strict morphological criteria. Crustacean hemiellipsoid bodies serve sensory integration functions and have been viewed as convergent with mushroom bodies. Only in land hermit crabs (Anomura) have learning/memory proteins been described in hemiellipsoid bodies, arranged in concentric layers with orthogonal networks comparable to insect mushroom body lobes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C28-C38 summarize prior knowledge about crustacean brain centers based on literature review and establish the novelty of the current findings. The claims about land hermit crabs (C33-C36) are supported by citations to previous work. These claims provide essential context for the significance of discovering mushroom bodies in stomatopods.

results.result: Mantis shrimps display sophisticated behaviors relating to predation, spatial memory, and visual recognition comparable to insects. They possess the most elaborate visual systems of any arthropod, frequent established hunting territories, form associative memories through multisensory integration, can be trained in discrimination-learning paradigms, and remember individual conspecifics.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C39-C47 describe stomatopod behavior and sensory capabilities based on multiple citations to behavioral and sensory studies. These claims establish the behavioral context that makes the presence of mushroom bodies in stomatopods particularly significant and provide motivation for the neuroanatomical investigation.

results.result: There is a conflict between neuroanatomy-based cladistics suggesting close phylogenetic proximity of insects and stomatopod crustaceans, and genomic evidence showing hexapods closely related to remipedes. Molecular phylogenies cannot provide reliable information about morphological changes since divergence. Similar cerebral arrangements in crustaceans and insects have been ascribed to convergent evolution, supported by fundamental differences in olfactory systems and the presence of hemiellipsoid bodies exclusively in crustaceans.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C48-C49, C118-C133 describe the phylogenetic context and conflict between morphological and molecular evidence. These claims are well-supported by citations to phylogenetic studies and comparative neuroanatomy. The discussion of methodological limitations (C121-C123) and examples of divergent brain evolution (C124-C126) provides important context for interpreting the significance of mushroom bodies in stomatopods.

results.result: Mushroom bodies have been identified in Myriapoda and Chelicerata, suggesting potential ubiquity across arthropods. In insects, mushroom bodies are characterized by high globuli cell packing density, clawed dendritic specializations, segmented synaptic domains along lobes, and dopaminergic neurons involved in conditioning. The calyxless condition in palaeopteran insects and Myriapoda, and developmental data showing lobe outgrowth preceding calyx development, suggest ancestral morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C72, C74, C79-C80, C85, C90, C92-C94 provide comparative context from other arthropod groups and developmental insights. These claims are supported by citations to comparative and developmental studies and help establish the broader phylogenetic distribution of mushroom bodies and the evolutionary significance of calyxless columns in stomatopods.

results.result: All crustaceans other than stomatopods lack mushroom bodies. Within more recently radiating eumalacostracan lineages, mushroom body morphology has undergone radical modification resulting in centers unrecognizable as mushroom bodies but retaining sensory integrator function. Fossil evidence and current results argue for an elaborate ancestral cerebral organization in the lower Cambrian.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53, C149 present major conclusions of the study based on the comparative survey (Result 4) and integration with fossil evidence. Claim C50 is supported by the survey data showing mushroom bodies only in stomatopods among crustaceans. Claim C51 is an interpretation of the evolutionary pattern observed in Result 4. Claims C52-C53 integrate fossil evidence with current findings to support an ancient origin hypothesis.

results.result: Each parallel fiber in stomatopods is assumed to contribute to local computational circuits within its column, by comparison to the Drosophila mushroom body lobe.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is an inference based on comparison with Drosophila (C69 cites Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017) but is not directly demonstrated in stomatopods. The assumption is reasonable given the anatomical similarities, but functional evidence would be needed to confirm that stomatopod parallel fibers actually perform similar computational roles.

results.result: Alpheid caridids (pistol shrimps) are the only group known to have evolved eusociality among crustaceans.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is a factual statement about pistol shrimp behavior that is consistent with known literature and is used to support the behavioral hypothesis in Result 8. This is established knowledge in crustacean behavioral ecology.
